title: Portrait and Hymn
premise: Emrys Villalobos, a reclusive urban explorer, discovers unmapped tunnels beneath the dying village of Hollowmere and learns they hum with a hymn whose bell was melted down in 1911. The song is an inheritance: every resident who hears its last verse must either sing it—joining the congregation of the drowned—or sign away their name to the last living resident, old Mrs. Aldery, who has kept the papers for a century. As Emrys maps the tunnels, he realizes his own family helped melt the bell to silence a massacre, and that staying invisible was the debt being paid all along. In the end, Emrys refuses both choices: he sings only the first two verses back into the dark, returning the song to those it was stolen from, and burns the papers, freeing the village at the cost of his own name.
about_author: Zephyrine Yarrow is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing parish records in abandoned Welsh mining villages before turning to fiction. They write horror about paperwork, bells, and the bureaucratic afterlife of small cruelties.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. He maps Hollowmere's storm drains at night, keeping meticulous counts of doors and lights, establishing his rules for invisibility. He finds a tunnel mouth no survey records, breathing warm air. Emotional beat: quiet competence curdling into unease when his door count comes back one too many.

chapters.title: One Door Too Many
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. He recounts every door in the village twice; the extra door stands where the church used to be, bricked over since 1911. Behind it, faintly, a bell tone. Emotional beat: the rationalist's denial as he blames his own counting, then checks a third time and gets a different number.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldery's Papers
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldery's POV. The last resident, ninety-six, reviews a leather folder of unsigned documents—one per villager, some yellowed to nothing. She practices signatures of people long dead. Emotional beat: weary duty; she is not villain but warden, waiting for someone to inherit the ledger.

chapters.title: The Bell That Was Melted
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. In the county archive he confirms the church bell was melted in 1911, sold as scrap after the 'choking winter.' The foundry record lists his great-grandfather among the workers. Emotional beat: inheritance as contamination—the past reaching up through his own surname.

chapters.title: First Ringing
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. At 3 a.m. the bell rings, though there is no bell. Every dog in the village goes silent instead of barking. Emrys watches the bricked doorway sweat mortar dust in rhythm. Emotional beat: terror disciplined into observation—he starts taking notes, which is its own kind of doom.

chapters.title: The Hymnal Fragment
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldery's POV. She gives Emrys a water-stained hymnal missing its final verse, torn out in 1911 by men who thought removing words would remove the debt. Emotional beat: her pity for him sharpening into something like hope that he might succeed where she chose not to try.

chapters.title: Down Where the Air Is Warm
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. He enters the unmapped tunnel, following the hymn's melody sung in many cracked voices. His lamp shows handprints on the walls, all pressed outward, as if from inside. Emotional beat: claustrophobic wonder—the dead are not attacking; they are rehearsing.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. His ritual of counting doors is revealed as inherited compulsion: his grandfather counted doors against the night the congregation vanished. Emrys realizes the habit wasn't safety—it was bookkeeping for the debt. Emotional beat: grief for a family that survived by serving.

chapters.title: The Choking Winter
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldery's POV, 1911 flashback. The village sealed the mine with the striking miners inside, sang a hymn to drown their cries, then melted the bell so the hymn could never be finished or answered. Emotional beat: complicity rendered intimate; she was a child holding the matches.

chapters.title: Verse One, Verse Two
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Reconstructing the hymn from archive fragments, he sings the first two verses aloud in the tunnel. The voices below fall silent, listening. Then something begins writing the third verse in condensation on the brick. Emotional beat: the intoxicating danger of being heard after years of hiding.

chapters.title: Sign Here
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldery's POV. A property developer arrives to buy the village; she slides the folder toward him. He signs eagerly—and walks into the church doorway that isn't there. Emotional beat: cold clarity; the papers don't save you, they just choose who pays.

chapters.title: What the Developer Left
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. He finds the developer's car running, doors locked, a signed contract on the seat with the signature still wet. The tunnel breathes warmer now. Emotional beat: dread shifting to resolve—Emrys stops documenting and starts deciding.

chapters.title: The Warden's Confession
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldery's POV. She tells Emrys the whole mechanism: the last verse sung completes the congregation's justice; the papers transfer the debt to a new name; she refused both for a century, keeping everyone in limbo. Emotional beat: shame transmuted into a plea—finish it, or free them, but end my watch.

chapters.title: Inheritance of Ash
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. He finds the foundry ledger page naming his great-grandfather, with a margin note: 'kept the crucible hot.' His family didn't just melt the bell—they kept the fire that unmade it. Emotional beat: fury at ancestors, and the vertigo of realizing he is the named heir.

chapters.title: The Congregation Below
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Deep in the tunnel he sees them: figures of soot and slag, mouths open mid-hymn, frozen since 1911. They are not ghosts demanding vengeance—they are a choir waiting for the note that will let them finish. Emotional beat: pity displacing fear; the horror is the pause, not the dead.

chapters.title: A Verse Is Not a Gift
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldery's POV. She warns him: whoever supplies the last verse becomes the bell—the instrument, rung forever. Her own brother tried in 1954. There is a second bell-shape in the tunnel wall. Emotional beat: love expressed as discouragement; she'd rather limbo than lose him too.

chapters.title: Third Verse, Found
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. In the flooded lower gallery he recovers the torn hymnal page, preserved in slag glass, the lost verse legible: a promise that the debt falls on the one who silenced the song. Reading it, he understands why the papers exist—to redirect it. Emotional beat: terrible clarity about what justice outside the law actually costs.

chapters.title: The Last Resident Signs
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldery's POV. Dying, she signs her own paper at last—not to escape but to hand Emrys the wardenship formally, making him the debtor of record. 'Now it's yours to refuse.' Emotional beat: release and burden in one stroke; her death quiets the village unnaturally.

chapters.title: Ringing
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. With the papers in his name, the bell rings continuously for three days. Doors multiply. The hymn rises to a shout. Emrys prepares: he copies the verse, writes his own name into the foundry ledger beside his great-grandfather's, and walks to the bricked door. Emotional beat: calm at the center of catastrophe—the explorer finally exploring himself.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, climax. At the threshold he sings the final verse—but alters the pronouns, singing it as the Villalobos heir, accepting the debt explicitly rather than letting it diffuse. The wall opens. The congregation finishes the hymn through him, and the sound is not vengeance but accounting: the bell tolls once for each name in the ledger, including his. Emotional beat: sacrifice as authorship—he chooses the sentence his family dodged.

chapters.title: Ash and Paper
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, falling action. The tunnel collapses inward, the bricked door becoming simply brick. Emrys survives but cannot remember his own name; the ledger burned with the debt paid. He keeps counting doors out of habit, and the count is always right now. Emotional beat: hollow peace—the price of survival was selfhood, and he paid it knowingly.

chapters.title: Hymn
chapters.summary: Epilogue, rotating brief POVs of villagers. Hollowmere empties gently; the church site grows wildflowers in a perfect rectangular patch. Someone new moves into Emrys's cottage and finds a hymnal with two verses and a note: 'Don't look for the third. It found me.' Far off, faintly, a bell that does not exist rings once, satisfied. Emotional beat: closure with a held breath—inherited debts end, but songs wait.
